messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Michael Hargrove, a 55-year-old single European American counselor, described a life that had narrowed around one evening at a community center where he had volunteered after work. During a heated dispute in the hallway, someone hurled a chair and a plastic bin across the room, and the sudden crash was followed by the sharp, burnt smell of an overheated electrical panel and the unmistakable odor of smoke drifting in from a small fire that had started behind a wall. Michael had been close enough to see people bolt for the exits, and though the fire was contained quickly, the chaos lodged in him as a man-made disaster that felt both sudden and absurdly close. In the weeks after, he found himself avoiding friends because invitations to dinner, bars, or even someone’s apartment brought him too near conversation about “that night,” and he had come to dread any setting where he might have to think about it. He also monitored his own thoughts with grim vigilance, checking constantly for signs that he was “going crazy,” because the event had left him convinced that if he let his mind wander toward it, he would not be able to handle what came next.  

What Michael noticed first was how his body seemed to betray him. He would catch a whiff of burnt toast from a neighbor’s kitchen or smoke from a passing truck and feel his chest tighten before he had time to tell himself he was safe. If someone nearby slammed a mug down, tossed a coat across a chair, or threw a set of keys onto a desk, his stomach lurched and he would scan the room for an exit without fully deciding to do so. Those cues pulled up more than alarm; they carried the event back into him in fragments. Sometimes, when he tried not to think about it, he would still be flooded by the same raw terror he had felt in the hallway, but without any clear picture of the faces, the room, or the sequence of what had happened. At other times he would suddenly smell smoke or singed wiring in his mind as vividly as if it were in front of him. The memory itself felt oddly detached, as if it belonged to another man entirely, someone he had watched rather than lived as himself. Because the sensations arrived so abruptly and stripped of context, Michael became more certain that his body was still reacting as if danger were present, and that the world could turn on him again without warning.  

That conviction did not stay abstract. Each time a smell or a thrown object jolted him, the memory came back stronger and more bodily, and the more it came back, the more threatening it felt. He began to think he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, and he interpreted every flare of panic as evidence that something was still wrong inside him. The more he braced himself against those moments, the more he felt trapped in the memory’s emotional intensity, especially when it rose without any image at all, leaving him shaken and ashamed in his office after a session or in the parking lot after work. He tried to avoid thinking about the event altogether, telling himself that even one deliberate effort to remember would overwhelm him, yet that avoidance offered little relief. Instead, the memory seemed to return in the background, shaped by the very effort to push it away, and he found himself watching his own mind for signs of breakdown with almost the same intensity that he watched doorways and hallways for danger.  

Over months, the pattern spread into his life as a counselor. Michael could still sit with clients, but after sessions he became reluctant to join colleagues for lunch, and he turned down long-standing plans with friends because he feared the casual talk might drift toward fires, violence, or “stressful experiences.” At home he avoided cooking when there was any chance of a burnt smell, and he kept windows open even in cold weather if he thought he might catch a whiff of smoke. Objects thrown in frustration—someone slapping a file onto a desk, a client tossing a pen, a neighbor throwing a bag into a dumpster—would spike him into the same unease that had first followed the disaster. Each time, he felt the old memory stir, and each time that stirred fear seemed to confirm his belief that his body was unreliable and that he remained on the edge of catastrophe. In that way his vigilance and his efforts to keep the event out of mind only kept the sensations alive, and the sensations kept convincing him that danger was still near. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted by the loop of smells, thrown objects, and internal monitoring, and he said what frightened him most was not only the memory itself but the fear that if he kept living this way, he would lose confidence in his own mind and his ability to remain the calm, competent man his work had always required.
